Revisiting scaling laws for reward optimization

Ali Aouad Affiliation: MIT Email: maouad@mit.edu    Aymane El Gadarri Affiliation: MIT Email: aymelgad@mit.edu    Vivek F. Farias Affiliation: MIT Email: vivekf@mit.edu
Abstract

Scaling laws for optimization against reward models in AI alignment have pinned down how performance depends on optimization effort---11 1 All dashes in this manuscript are human generated.measured by a KL-divergence budget relative to a reference policy. Beyond a certain budget, over-optimization (or reward hacking) can arise: because we optimize against a proxy reward model (distinct from true rewards), performance can plateau or degrade. Naturally, the proxy reward’s accuracy depends on how much preference data (often in the form of pairwise comparisons) was used to train it. However, existing research does not cleanly identify how performance jointly scales with the amount of training data and the divergence budget. Our main contribution is to provide an empirically accurate and theoretically grounded scaling law in such context. Performance roughly scales as Θ⁡(min⁡{log⁡(M),K})\Theta(\sqrt{\min\{\log(M),K\}}), where MM is the number of comparisons in training data and KK is the policy’s divergence budget. We develop an information-theoretic model to establish this upper bound and prove it is tightly achievable through a constructive procedure. Informed by this, we conduct extensive empirical evaluations using a real-world annotation setup, whereby a large 70B gold reward model generates feedback data and proxy reward models are trained from less capable models (0.6B to 4B). Our scaling law provides an excellent fit (R2 from 97% to 99%), outperforms alternative specifications, and remains robust across model sizes, noise, and optimization procedures (best-of-NN or policy tilting). Our evidence suggests that reward optimization is analogous to a surprisingly simple selection task: choosing from a sequence of IID Gaussian random variables using noisy preference feedback.

1 Introduction

Post-training typically entails learning, either explicitly or implicitly, a proxy ‘reward’ model of user preferences (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023). Such a model remains an imperfect proxy of true user preferences, learned from limited data. As such, it is natural that ‘over-optimizing’ against such a proxy model may eventually lead to a decrease in the performance gained from post training (Manheim and Garrabrant, 2018; Skalse et al., 2022). A seminal paper by Gao et al. (2023) established empirical scaling laws for this phenomenon. They showed that performance first increased like the square root of the divergence of the post-trained policy from the pre-trained policy, and then beyond some specific divergence budget, performance stalled or decreased. With the advent of long running agents, one only expects such a problem to be exacerbated, potentially leading to catastrophic outcomes (Marklund et al., 2026). This has been the topic of much recent research on superalignment. A consensus recipe that has emerged from the above research is that any post-trained policy should be constrained to within some pre-specified divergence budget of a reference policy to prevent over-optimization. While previous literature extensively studies tradeoffs between achievable performance and divergence budget, its dependence on the amount of preference data is not well-understood. This raises the natural question:

How should the policy divergence budget be set as a function of the amount of data used to train the proxy reward model?

It is natural, in particular, that a proxy model trained on limited preference data is more susceptible to over-optimization than one trained with a lot of such data. As such, we seek scaling laws that capture the amount data used to train the proxy reward model. In particular, we would like these scaling laws to inform the performance improvement this data affords us relative to a reference policy. In addition, we wish to characterize how the aforementioned divergence budget ought to be scaled with the amount of preference data. Answering these questions can provide important insights to clarify the fundamental limits of post-training and guide algorithmic scaling recipes in AI alignment.

Contributions.

Our work provides a theoretical and empirical characterization of how post-training performance jointly scales with the amount of preference data and the divergence budget.

  • •

    Simple theoretical derivation. We develop an information-theoretic model that guides our subsequent empirical evaluations. The model yields a tight scaling law, roughly of the form Θ⁡(min⁡{log⁡(M),K})\Theta(\sqrt{\min\{\log(M),K\}}), where MM is the number of preference comparisons in the training dataset (scale of feedback data) and KK is the KL-divergence budget (optimization effort). We give constructive procedures that near-optimally attain this bound.

  • •

    Accurate empirical scaling law. We provide extensive empirical evidence that our post-training scaling law is highly accurate and provides a statistically better fit than alternative specifications, focusing on the novel predicted dependence Θ⁡(log⁡M)\Theta(\sqrt{\log M}) on the amount of preference data. We use a real-world annotation setup whereby a large 70B model (serving as the gold reward model) generates preference data while proxy reward models are trained on these data using smaller models. The scaling law is robust across optimization procedures, noisy preferences, and model sizes.

  • •

    Conceptual insight. Our evidence in support of this scaling law connects post-training to a surprisingly simple selection problem: choosing among a sequence of IID Gaussian random variables from noisy preference data.

2 Related Literature

Alignment and overoptimization.

Overoptimization of a misspecified objective function (or reward hacking) is a long-standing concern in AI alignment (Wiener, 1960; Leike et al., 2017). Overoptimization can be defined as a regime in which increasing proxy reward strictly decreases true reward—an extreme form of Goodhart’s Law whereby optimization against a certain metric erodes its efficacy (Manheim and Garrabrant, 2018). To counter this, Skalse et al. (2022) define a natural notion of unhackable rewards but find that it implies a very restrictive condition: any nontrivial unhackable rewards must induce the same policy ordering. In MDPs, Karwowski et al. (2024) give a geometric explanation of how the proxy and true-optimal policies diverge once optimization pushes the occupancy measure to a face of the polytope where the two rewards disagree. While this strand of literature focuses on mechanisms leading to overoptimization, we instead focus on quantifying its effect on achievable performance. Closer to us, Marklund et al. (2026) study a selection model in which an agent optimizing a consequentialist objective over a large outcome space incurs catastrophic performance with high probability. Our model shares the outcome selection set-up and information-theoretic approach, but we separate policy divergence and preference data budgets and construct policies that achieve matching lower bounds. Our goal is eventually to develop accurate scaling laws.

Post-training scaling laws.

Gao et al. (2023) provide the closest empirical antecedent to this work: in a synthetic setup where a fixed gold reward model stands in for human annotators, they measure gold reward as a function of KL-divergence from the base policy and find that it rises like K\sqrt{K} and then declines. However, while they vary the size of the preference dataset, they do not identify an explicit scaling law in that dimension.22 2 Quoting the authors, “The scaling of α\alpha and β\beta with data size are not as cleanly described as for RM size scaling.” An inverted-U shape also uncovered for direct policy optimization setups without a reward model (Rafailov et al., 2024). Pessimistic adjustments and robust ensembling methods can mitigate the perverse effects of overoptimization (Coste et al., 2024; Eisenstein et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025). However, previous research often take the proxy model as exogenous and do not ask what specific divergence budget the preference data they are trained on can support. The dependence on K\sqrt{K} can be traced back to analyses of selection bias for adaptive data analyses (Russo and Zou, 2016). Related work on AI alignment further characterizes tradeoffs between reward maximization and policy distribution shift (Mroueh, 2024; Laidlaw et al., 2025) under assumptions on the proxy rewards. Still, these works treat the underlying data as exogenous; in our language, the scaling is with respect to KK but it does not make explicit the dependence on the amount of preference data MM. Instead our work reveals how information obtained from preference data constrains attainable rewards.

Learning from comparisons.

The proxy in equation 1 is fit to pairwise preferences under a Bradley–Terry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952; Christiano et al., 2017). Zhu et al. (2023) give the first sample complexity bounds for this pipeline, showing that the MLE converges for linear rewards under Bradley–Terry–Luce and Plackett–Luce, but that a policy trained on the plain MLE can fail while a pessimistic MLE succeeds under a coverage condition. This literature bounds how well MM comparisons pin down the reward; we instead ask how much reward gain MM comparisons can support at all, irrespective of the estimator. Closest to the combinatorial side of our question is work on selection from noisy comparisons: Falahatgar et al. (2017) establish the comparison complexity of identifying an approximate maximum, and Chen and Suh (2015) that of top-KK recovery, with rates governed by the approximation tolerance and the gap at the top-KK boundary, respectively. However, these works do not explicitly quantify the corresponding expected reward gain nor they account for divergence constraints.

3 Model and Results

Consider the following setup for alignment. For a prompt–response pair (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, human preferences are encoded by a gold reward r⁡(x,y)r(x,y) that is never observed. In its place we have a proxy r^​(x,y)\hat{r}(x,y), calibrated on a dataset of MM pairwise comparisons: for triples (x,y,y′)(x,y,y^{\prime}), an annotator reports which of y,y′y,y^{\prime} is preferred. Given a base policy π0\pi_{0} that assigns to each prompt a distribution over responses, an aligned policy π^K\hat{\pi}_{K} optimizes the proxy against a divergence budget,

maxπ𝔼x,π[r^(x,y)]subject to𝔼x[DKL(π(⋅∣x)∥π0(⋅∣x))]≤K.\max_{\pi}\;\mathbb{E}_{x,\,\pi}\!\left[\hat{r}(x,y)\right]\quad\text{subject to}\quad\mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi(\cdot\mid x)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x)\right)\right]\;\leq\;K. (1)

KK constrains optimization pressure. Because r^\hat{r} is an imperfect proxy, driving expected proxy reward upward eventually drives expected gold reward downward. Writing R⁡(K):=𝔼x,π^K​[r⁡(x,y)]R(K):=\mathbb{E}_{x,\,\hat{\pi}_{K}}[r(x,y)] for the gold reward earned by the aligned policy, Gao et al. (2023) establish an empirical scaling law: R⁡(K)R(K) initially behaves like K\sqrt{K}, and beyond some K⋆K^{\star} is decreasing in KK.

The proxy is itself calibrated from MM comparisons, so both R⁡(⋅)R(\cdot) and K⋆K^{\star} must depend on MM; the scaling law of Gao et al. (2023) does not address how. We seek to answer two related practical questions. First, how does the scaling law depend on MM for a given KK, and in particular, how should the divergence budget KK be set as a function of MM? And second, what gold reward gain over the base policy does the resulting policy earn?

3.1 An Information-Theoretic Setup

We propose here a simplified setup that will allow us to make theoretical progress on our questions; candidate scaling laws obtained from the analysis of this setup are then evaluated in the empirical setup of Gao et al. (2023) in §5. For a universe of nn potential responses, indexed by ii, we associate with each an independent gold reward Ri∼𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)R_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}). We model a prompt as an admissible set A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n], with Pr⁡(i∈A)=p\Pr(i\in A)=p independently across ii. Here AA is the set of responses that are candidate answers to the realized prompt, and pp is the fraction of the universe a prompt renders relevant.33 3 If A=∅A=\varnothing we allow a dummy fallback action 00 with deterministic reward R0=μR_{0}=\mu. We remark that this setup is close to one studied recently by Marklund et al. (2026).

A preference dataset contains a label Yi​jY_{ij} for each pair (i,j)(i,j) in a set EE of MM response pairs. The dataset is deterministic when Yi​j=𝟏{Ri>Rj}Y_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\{R_{i}>R_{j}\}, and random when the labels are sampled conditionally on the rewards. We write T:={(i,j,Yi​j):(i,j)∈E}T:=\{(i,j,Y_{ij}):(i,j)\in E\} for the dataset.

Assumption 1 (Information Structure).

We assume that E⟂(R,A)E\perp(R,A) so that the pairs in the preference dataset are chosen without future knowledge of the admissible set or information about RR. Moreover, A⟂(R,T)A\perp(R,T).

We let π0(⋅∣A,E)\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid A,E) be an arbitrary reward-blind base policy. Specifically, an AA-valued random variable JJ distributed according to π0(⋅∣A,E)\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid A,E) is dependent on AA and potentially, EE but independent of RR. Consequently, 𝔼π0​[RJ]=μ\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{0}}[R_{J}]=\mu. An informed policy π(⋅∣T,A)\pi(\cdot\mid T,A) selects an index J∈AJ\in A after seeing the preference dataset TT and the admissible set AA. Define the expected policy divergence and the reward gain by

K(π;π0)≜𝔼[DKL(π(⋅∣T,A)∥π0(⋅∣A,E))],Δ(π)≜𝔼π[RJ]−μ.K(\pi;\pi_{0})\;\triangleq\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi(\cdot\mid T,A)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid A,E)\right)\right],\qquad\Delta(\pi)\;\triangleq\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[R_{J}]-\mu. (2)

We next present our results; taken together they provide a theoretical answer to the practical questions posed above.

3.2 A Preview of Our Results

We present here an informal overview of our key result, which holds for both deterministic and random preference datasets:

Theorem (Informal).

Suppose K⁡(π,π0)≤KK(\pi;\pi_{0})\leq K and |E|≤M|E|\leq M. Then, for any such π\pi,

Δ⁡(π)≲σ​2​min⁡{K,log⁡(p​M)}.\Delta(\pi)\;\lesssim\;\sigma\sqrt{2\min\{K,\log(pM)\}}.

Moreover, there exists a preference dataset EE and a resulting proxy r^\hat{r} for which the optimized policy π\pi satisfies

Δ⁡(π)≳(1−o⁡(1))​σ​2​min⁡{K,log⁡(p​M)}.\Delta(\pi)\;\gtrsim\;(1-o(1))\,\sigma\sqrt{2\min\{K,\log(p\sqrt{M})\}}.

The asymptotic regime implicit in the statements above requires that min⁡{K,log⁡(p​M)}\min\{K,\log(p\sqrt{M})\} grow large.44 4 The dependence on pp is not central to our analysis; pp is a stylized measure of how much overlap there is in the admissible responses of distinct prompts—a notion of how well preference data generalizes across prompts. That is, the regime is one where both the divergence budget, and the effective number of comparisons for a prompt grows. We briefly discuss the implications of the above result here. First, observe that the lower and upper bounds on Δ⁡(π)\Delta(\pi) are tight: they are within a constant factor of 2\sqrt{2} of each other. As such, the bounds explain precisely the K\sqrt{K} scaling law established by Gao et al. (2023). The bounds also prescribe how to pick the divergence budget KK: specifically, we want K∼log⁡(p​M)K\sim\log(pM): any slower and we leave improvement opportunities on the table; any faster and we risk over-optimizing against the proxy. The next section formalizes the above theorem and presents its proof, following which we turn to empirically verifying that the above result holds in a (larger scale) variant of the scaling law study performed by Gao et al. (2023).

4 Scaling laws for reward optimization

4.1 Reward optimization scaling law under deterministic preferences

We now make the preceding bounds precise. We allow the informed policy to use the comparison data directly, so our upper bound applies regardless of how a proxy is fit. For the lower bound, we construct a proxy and a base policy that attain the stated gain. Write r^​(i,T)\hat{r}(i;T) for the proxy reward assigned to response ii using the comparison data TT. As in equation 1, the aligned policy π^K\hat{\pi}_{K} maximizes expected proxy reward within divergence budget KK.

We assume for simplicity that n≥2​Mn\geq\sqrt{2M} throughout the analysis. This ensures enough possible responses for our construction and leaves the scaling law in MM and KK unchanged. In practice, it is plausible to assume that the number of possible responses is much larger than our preference dataset.

Theorem 2 (Deterministic preferences).

Under the information structure above, every reward-blind base policy π0\pi_{0}, deterministic preference dataset generated on pairs EE with |E|≤M|E|\leq M, and informed policy with K⁡(π,π0)≤KK(\pi;\pi_{0})\leq K must satisfy

Δ⁡(π)≤σ​2​min⁡{K,log⁡(1+2​p​M)}.\Delta(\pi)\leq\sigma\sqrt{2\min\{K,\log(1+2pM)\}}. (3)

Reciprocally, there is a universal constant c>0c>0 such that, whenever p​2​M≥4p\sqrt{2M}\geq 4, for every K≥0K\geq 0 there exist a set of comparison pairs EE with |E|≤M|E|\leq M, a reward-blind base policy, and a proxy such that, for the resulting deterministic preference dataset, every optimizer π^K\hat{\pi}_{K} satisfies

Δ⁡(π^K)≥c​σ​min⁡{K,log⁡(p​2​M)}.\Delta(\hat{\pi}_{K})\geq c\,\sigma\sqrt{\min\{K,\log(p\sqrt{2M})\}}. (4)

The common upper bound is proved below, the lower-bound construction is given in Appendix A.2.

4.2 The same scaling law holds under noisy preferences

So far, we assumed that preferences were deterministic: a response is recorded as preferred whenever it has the larger gold reward. In reality, preference data is noisy. For each (i,j)∈E(i,j)\in E, let Yi​j=1Y_{ij}=1 indicate that ii is preferred to jj. As is standard in RLHF, we model preference labels with the Bradley–Terry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952):

Pr⁡(Yi​j=1∣R,E)=11+exp(−(Ri−Rj)/β),β>0.\Pr(Y_{ij}=1\mid R,E)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-(R_{i}-R_{j})/\beta)},\qquad\beta>0. (5)

Here β>0\beta>0 controls the preference noise: larger β\beta makes labels less sensitive to reward differences. The finite-budget lower bound now depends on β/σ\beta/\sigma, the noise scale relative to the variation in gold rewards.

Theorem 3 (Noisy preferences).

Suppose preferences follow the Bradley-Terry model with conditionally independent labels and noise scale β>0\beta>0. Under the information structure above, every reward-blind base policy π0\pi_{0}, random preference dataset generated on pairs EE with |E|≤M|E|\leq M, and informed policy with K⁡(π,π0)≤KK(\pi;\pi_{0})\leq K satisfy

Δ⁡(π)≤σ​2​min⁡{K,log⁡(1+2​p​M)}.\Delta(\pi)\leq\sigma\sqrt{2\min\{K,\log(1+2pM)\}}. (6)

Reciprocally, there is a constant c⁡(β/σ)>0c(\beta/\sigma)>0, depending only on β/σ\beta/\sigma, such that, whenever p​2​M≥4p\sqrt{2M}\geq 4, for every K≥0K\geq 0 there exist a set of comparison pairs EE with |E|≤M|E|\leq M, a reward-blind base policy, and a proxy such that, for the resulting random preference dataset, every optimizer π^K\hat{\pi}_{K} satisfies

Δ⁡(π^K)≥c⁡(β/σ)​σ​min⁡{K,log⁡(p​2​M)}.\Delta(\hat{\pi}_{K})\geq c(\beta/\sigma)\,\sigma\sqrt{\min\{K,\log(p\sqrt{2M})\}}. (7)

Both lower bounds fix a set of m=⌊2​M⌋m=\lfloor\sqrt{2M}\rfloor responses and compare each pair once, using (m2)≤M\binom{m}{2}\leq M comparisons. Deterministic preferences reveal the order of these responses by gold reward. With noisy preferences, we score each response by the fraction of its m−1m-1 comparisons in which it is preferred. Within any nonempty subset of these responses, we then select the response with the highest score. For fixed σ,β>0\sigma,\beta>0, the expected gap between its gold reward and the largest gold reward in that subset tends to zero as mm grows. Appendix A.3 gives the full finite-budget argument. We prove the common upper bound below.

Proof.

Consider a preference dataset generated on a possibly random pair set EE, with |E|≤M|E|\leq M, and an informed policy π\pi satisfying K⁡(π,π0)≤KK(\pi;\pi_{0})\leq K. Both arguments below apply to deterministic preferences and to the Bradley–Terry model.

The divergence budget.

Let PπP_{\pi} and P0P_{0} denote the joint laws of (R,E,T,A,J)(R,E,T,A,J) under π\pi and π0\pi_{0}. These laws differ only in the conditional distribution of the chosen JJ. The chain rule for relative entropy therefore gives

DKL(Pπ∥P0)=𝔼[DKL(π(⋅∣T,A)∥π0(⋅∣A,E))]≤K.D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\pi}\|P_{0})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi(\cdot\mid T,A)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid A,E)\right)\right]\leq K.

𝔼P0​[et⁡(RJ−μ)]=Pr⁡(A=∅)+Pr⁡(A≠∅)​et2​σ2/2≤et2​σ2/2.\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\!\left[e^{t(R_{J}-\mu)}\right]=\Pr(A=\varnothing)+\Pr(A\neq\varnothing)e^{t^{2}\sigma^{2}/2}\leq e^{t^{2}\sigma^{2}/2}.

The size of the preference dataset.

Let V⁡(E)V(E) be the set of responses appearing in EE, so |V⁡(E)|≤2​M|V(E)|\leq 2M. Conditional on EE, the labels depend only on rewards in V⁡(E)V(E) and, in the noisy model, independent preference randomness. Corollary 4 (Asymptotic bound on performance).

Fix σ>0\sigma>0 and, for Bradley–Terry preferences, β>0\beta>0. Under either preference model, along any sequence (n,M,p,K)(n,M,p,K) with K→∞K\to\infty and p​2​M→∞p\sqrt{2M}\to\infty, there exist a pair set EE with |E|≤M|E|\leq M, a reward-blind base policy, and a proxy such that, for the resulting preference dataset, every optimizer π^K\hat{\pi}_{K} satisfies

5 Experiments

5.1 Summary

In this section, we evaluate our proposed scaling law empirically and test its accuracy against other specifications. We use a real-world annotation set-up and generate preference data from a large gold reward model. We train proxy reward models with 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B parameters and compare alternative scaling functions. The square-root-logarithmic form fits well across model sizes, preference noise, and optimization methods. It significantly outperforms linear and square-root growth in all tested settings

5.2 Setup

Models and data.

Following Gao et al. (2023), we study reward optimization using preferences supplied by a fixed gold reward model, Llama-3.3-Nemotron-70B-Reward. Our proxies are Qwen3 base models with 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B parameters, each with a scalar reward head. Our training corpus contains 1,000 first-turn prompts from the Arena 140K dataset LMArena (2025), a highly diverse dataset spanning code, mathematics, and other topics (the full mixture is described in Appendix B.1). We sample 600 responses per prompt from the fixed reference policy Qwen3-4B-Instruct at temperature 1.

Preference data.

We construct 300 disjoint response pairs per prompt, summing to 300,000 offline comparisons in our largest dataset. We exclude identical-response pairs and duplicate text pairs. In the noiseless setting, the response with highest gold reward is preferred, with exact ties broken uniformly, as in Gao et al. (2023). For the noisy-label experiments, we sample a Bradley-Terry preference with probability Pr⁡(ya≻yb∣x)=σ⁡(r⁡(x,ya)−r⁡(x,yb))\Pr(y_{a}\succ y_{b}\mid x)=\sigma(r(x,y_{a})-r(x,y_{b})).

Training and comparison budgets.

The main scaling experiment increases MM from 600 to 300,000 by expanding the set of prompts in a fixed, reward-independent order, while holding the number of comparisons per prompt at 300. We fine-tune all parameters for one pass using the pairwise logistic loss and AdamW at constant learning rate 10−510^{-5}. Each policy update contains 600 comparisons from two complete prompt groups.

Evaluation.

We evaluate on 128 prompts disjoint from training, with 8,192 responses each. Best-of-NN selects the highest-proxy-reward response among NN candidates. We sweep logarithmically spaced NN up to 8,192, corresponding to the conventional optimization-pressure coordinate KN=log⁡N−(N−1)/NK_{N}=\log N-(N-1)/N (Gao et al., 2023). We estimate gold and proxy rewards using the unbiased subset-average estimator of Nakano et al. (2021, Appendix I), which highly reduces the variance of the estimates. Reward gains are measured relative to the mean reward at N=1N=1 over the full response pool for each prompt, and are normalized by a fixed reference gold standard deviation.

5.3 The peak reward follows the predicted square root logarithmic scaling

The comparison-limited regime of Section 3.2 predicts square-root-logarithmic growth of achievable gold-reward gains. We first test this scaling by varying the size of preference dataset MM sizes from 600600 to 300,000300,000. For each trained proxy reward (MM), we determine the best-of-N response model, varying N∈𝒢N\in\mathcal{G} in our evaluated grid bounded by N≤8,192N\leq 8{,}192. We tune NN as the observed peak of Δ^max​(M)=maxN∈𝒢⁡Δ^M​(N)\widehat{\Delta}_{\max}(M)=\max_{N\in\mathcal{G}}\widehat{\Delta}_{M}(N), where Δ^M​(N)\widehat{\Delta}_{M}(N) is the mean standardized gold-reward gain.

Figure 1 shows that the peak gold reward closely follows the predicted scaling law. Figure 2 compares the predicted form with affine fits a+b​f​(M)a+bf(M) using the same models and two free parameters for every function. The square-root-logarithmic form gives the best fit, with R2=0.992R^{2}=0.992, compared with 0.990, 0.803, and 0.571 for log⁡M\log M, M\sqrt{M}, and MM, respectively.

Table 1 summarizes the fits across proxy sizes, preference noise, and optimization methods, which we examine below.

5.4 Robustness to the optimization algorithm

We test robustness to the optimization algorithm by replacing best-of-NN selection with exponential tilting, an idealized form of KL-regularized reinforcement learning that approximates its optimal policy using samples from the reference policy. For inverse temperature β>0\beta>0, the objective maxπ{𝔼π[r^M]−β−1DKL(π∥π0)}\max_{\pi}\{\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\hat{r}_{M}]-\beta^{-1}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi_{0})\} has the exponentially tilted optimizer πβ,M​(y∣x)∝π0​(y∣x)​exp⁡(β​r^M​(x,y))\pi_{\beta,M}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{0}(y\mid x)\exp(\beta\hat{r}_{M}(x,y)) (Rafailov et al., 2023). We approximate this policy using responses from the reference policy. The same exponential reweighting is used in soft best-of-NN sampling to approximate KL-regularized alignment (Verdun et al., 2025), including empirical studies with imperfect reward models (Aminian et al., 2025).

For each evaluation prompt xx, we place uniform reference mass on its S=8,192S=8{,}192 sampled responses and assign the tilted policy weights

wβ,M,i​(x)=exp⁡(β​r^M​(x,yi))∑j=1Sexp⁡(β​r^M​(x,yj)).w_{\beta,M,i}(x)=\frac{\exp\!\left(\beta\hat{r}_{M}(x,y_{i})\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{S}\exp\!\left(\beta\hat{r}_{M}(x,y_{j})\right)}. (9)

We compute the weighted gold reward and conditional KL exactly on each pool, averaging over the same test prompts and retaining the gold-reward normalization from Section 5.2.

The right column of Figure 5 in Appendix C shows the same square-root-logarithmic scaling under exponential tilting.

5.5 Robustness to preference noise

We next test robustness to preference noise using the Bradley–Terry–Luce (BTL) model (Bradley and Terry, 1952). Labels are drawn once and held fixed throughout training, 33.6% of the 300,000 labels differ from their noiseless counterparts. For each model size, we keep the same model initialization, comparison stream, and evaluation pools, so the comparison isolates the effect of preference noise. Panels (c), (d), (g), and (h) of Figure 5 show that the square-root-logarithmic trend persists under noisy preferences.

The fit is slightly less tight than in the noiseless setting, its agreement with the scaling predicted by our theory is on par with the theory’s expected behavior for noisy labels. In particular, the noisy-label theorem predicts the same square-root-logarithmic scaling, but only in a higher-comparison regime. We hypothesize that in practice, additional samples are needed for the noise to average out and for the asymptotic scaling to emerge more cleanly.

5.6 Robustness to proxy model size

Finally, we increase the proxy size from 0.6B to 1.7B and 4B parameters within the Qwen3 base-model family. Both proxies use the same noiseless preferences, comparison order, and evaluation pools.

Table 1 shows that the square-root-logarithmic form remains the best fit among the four specifications for both larger proxies and both optimization methods. For 1.7B, R2=0.989R^{2}=0.989 under both methods; for 4B, R2=0.972R^{2}=0.972 under best-of-NN and 0.9700.970 under tilting. The paired prediction tests also favor this form over log⁡M\log M, M\sqrt{M}, and MM for both larger proxies under both methods, with Holm-adjusted p<0.05p<0.05 in each comparison.

6 Conclusion

Our work provides a theoretical and empirical characterization of how post-training performance scales jointly with preference data and optimization effort. A simple information-theoretic model yields the scaling OPENmin⁡(log⁡(M),KCLOSE)\sqrt{\min(\log(M),K}) , with constructive procedures that attain this order. Our experiments show that the predicted dependence on preference data provides a strong fit across model sizes, noisy preferences, and optimization procedures. Extending the theory to more general reward distributions and adaptive preference collection, and testing the scaling with human preferences and policy training, are natural directions for future work.

A.2 Proof of Theorem 2

It remains to prove the lower bound. We first relate proxy optimization to the construction, then establish its feasibility and reward gain.

The proxy.

For either preference model, take r^​(i,T)=𝔼⁡[Ri∣T]\hat{r}(i;T)=\mathbb{E}[R_{i}\mid T], with r^​(0,T)=μ\hat{r}(0;T)=\mu. Since A⟂(R,T)A\perp(R,T), every informed policy satisfies

𝔼πRJ=𝔼[∑iπ(i∣T,A)𝔼[Ri∣T,A]]=𝔼πr^(J;T).\mathbb{E}_{\pi}R_{J}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i}\pi(i\mid T,A)\mathbb{E}[R_{i}\mid T,A]\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\hat{r}(J;T). (10)

It therefore suffices to construct a feasible informed policy with the claimed gain. An optimizer exists for the following reason. There are only finitely many possible pairs (T,A)(T,A): the dataset records pair identities and binary labels, and A⊆[n]A\subseteq[n]. Ignore pairs of probability zero. A policy is then specified by finitely many choice probabilities. A finite divergence budget requires π⁡(i∣T,A)=0\pi(i\mid T,A)=0 whenever π0​(i∣A,E)=0\pi_{0}(i\mid A,E)=0. The remaining probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one for each (T,A)(T,A), so their domain is compact. On this domain, the divergence is continuous: each term x​log⁡(x/b)x\log(x/b) with b>0b>0 extends continuously to zero by assigning it the value zero. Hence the budget constraint defines a closed subset of this compact domain. The feasible set is nonempty because it contains π0\pi_{0}. Finally, expected proxy reward is a continuous linear function of the choice probabilities, so it must attain its maximum on the feasible set.

For the remainder of the proof, write

m=⌊2​M⌋,q=p​2​M,h=min⁡{K,log⁡q}.m=\lfloor\sqrt{2M}\rfloor,\qquad q=p\sqrt{2M},\qquad h=\min\{K,\log q\}.

For K≥log⁡2K\geq\log 2, set s=min⁡{N,⌊eK⌋}s=\min\{N,\lfloor e^{K}\rfloor\}. The upper bound follows from Appendix A.1. For the lower bound, remember the set SS, base policy, and notation from Appendix A.2, with q≥4q\geq 4. Appendix B Additional Experimental Details

B.1 Data construction and topic composition

We use English first-turn prompts from LMArena’s arena-human-preference-140k. The final training set contains 1,000 prompts, each contributing 300 disjoint response pairs and hence 600 retained responses. Responses are sampled from Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with temperature 1, top-p=1p=1, no top-kk restriction, and at most 1,024 new tokens. Pair construction excludes identical responses and repeated text pairs, additional responses are sampled when necessary to obtain 300 eligible pairs.

Table 2 gives the prompt-topic distribution.

B.2 Conditional gold-reward distributions

The theoretical model in Section 3.1 assumes Gaussian rewards. We examine this idealization using the empirical distribution of gold scores within individual prompts. Each example uses all 8,192 responses in its test-prompt pool, scored by the fixed gold reward model before best-of-NN selection.

We choose four prompts independently of their reward values. The examples concern AutoHotkey scrolling, a modal-logic agent, motivational story topics, and railway recruitment exam questions.

For a prompt with scores r1,…,rnr_{1},\ldots,r_{n}, let r¯=n−1​∑iri\bar{r}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}r_{i} and s2=n−1​∑i(ri−r¯)2s^{2}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}(r_{i}-\bar{r})^{2}. The normal Q–Q plot compares the ordered standardized scores z(i)=(r(i)−r¯)/sz_{(i)}=(r_{(i)}-\bar{r})/s with

qi=Φ−1(i−1/2n),i=1,…,n,q_{i}=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{i-1/2}{n}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n, (26)

where Φ\Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Gaussian scores would approximately follow the line z=qz=q.

Figures 3 and 4 show that the conditional gold-reward distributions need not be Gaussian. All four examples have negative empirical skewness, ranging from −0.75-0.75 to −0.22-0.22. The creative-writing example has the strongest asymmetry, with skewness −0.75-0.75 and excess kurtosis 1.191.19. Departures from the reference line in the Q–Q plots reveal differences in distributional shape even after matching each prompt’s mean and variance. Thus, the empirical scaling results arise in a setting whose reward distributions depart from the Gaussian idealization.

B.3 Hyperparameters

We found reward-model training to work over a broad range of learning rates in preliminary sweeps, from 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} to 4×10−54\times 10^{-5}, consistent with the findings of Ouyang et al. (2022, Appendix C.2). We then compared 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} and 10−510^{-5} in 75,000-comparison pilots, selecting by final logistic loss on 512 validation comparisons from 64 held-out prompts distinct from training and test sets. All validations selected 10−510^{-5}, which we use for the scaling experiments; Coste et al. (2024) use the same reward-model learning rate. Table 3 gives the complete shared settings.
